posts.title: Before the scaffold is erected: the temporary works checks that keep the load path intact
posts.excerpt: A 14 October 2026 Construction Magazine / London Construction Magazine article sets out the temporary works checks that should be completed before scaffolding is erected. A scaffold that is correctly designed in isolation can still be unsuitable if the ground, supporting structure, façade, services, attachments or foreseeable alterations do not match the assumptions in the design brief. BS 5975-1:2024 places the design brief at the centre of control so that interfaces, reactions and change are captured before erection begins.

On 14 October 2026 Construction Magazine / London Construction Magazine published practical guidance on the temporary works checks that matter before scaffolding is erected. The design brief under BS 5975-1:2024 is the point at which intended use, loading class, boarded lifts, loading bays, ties, sheeting, hoists, temporary roofs, ground conditions and interfaces should be captured. Maximum leg reactions must be known so that the supporting ground or structure can be assessed. Subsurface features such as basements, drains, manholes or soft patches require specific consideration rather than an assumption that the surface is adequate. Tie strategy must suit the actual façade, including openings, weak masonry or planned removals. Attachments that alter wind loading or reactions should be identified before erection, not added later. Foreseeable changes must be routed through the project temporary works procedure.

HSE scaffolding guidance requires either a recognised standard configuration or a design by a competent person, and that the foundation is capable of carrying the loads. The Temporary Works Coordinator role under BS 5975 is an effective way of ensuring those requirements are coordinated.

body.p: On 14 October 2026 Construction Magazine / London Construction Magazine published “Before Scaffolding Is Erected: The Temporary Works Checks That Matter”. The article states that before a scaffold is erected the project team needs to know more than its height, length and intended access route. A scaffold can be correctly designed in isolation and still be unsuitable for the site if the ground, supporting structure, façade, services, attachments or future alterations do not match the assumptions used in that design. Problems commonly arise when elements are considered separately: leg loads bearing over a basement or void, increased reactions from a loading bay, mismatched tie patterns after façade removal, or wind actions from sheeting or temporary roofs that were not in the original brief. The current management procedures for temporary works are set out in BS 5975-1:2024. For project teams operating a BS 5975 procedure, the design brief is the point where requirements and interfaces should be captured before design progresses. Pre-erection checks cover design status (compliance sheet or project-specific design and check), intended loading, maximum leg reactions, foundation condition (including subsurface features), ties and anchors matched to the actual façade, attachments that affect loading or wind, site interfaces, and a change-control process.

Scaffolding is temporary works. HSE scaffolding guidance requires a scaffold either to follow a recognised standard configuration or, where it falls outside such a configuration, to be designed by calculation by a competent person. The foundation must be capable of carrying the scaffold and the loads placed on it; basements, drains and patches of soft ground that may collapse when loaded are specifically highlighted. CDM 2015 requires the principal contractor to plan, manage and monitor the construction phase and contractors to plan, manage and monitor their own work. BS 5975-1:2024 provides the industry framework for temporary works management procedures (it is not a statute). Exact clause references should be confirmed against the project’s licensed copy. The design brief is the control point that brings together use, loads, reactions, ground or structural support, ties, attachments and foreseeable change so that the load path from the scaffold through bases and ties into the supporting ground or structure is coherent. Standard does not automatically mean low risk when site conditions differ from the assumptions behind a standard configuration. Provisional category only — to be confirmed by the TWC and the project temporary works procedure.

body.h: Practical TWC and TWS control points
ul: Capture in the design brief the intended use, loading class, boarded lifts, material storage, loading bays, ties, sheeting/netting, hoists, debris chutes, temporary roofs, ground conditions, subsurface features, façade type and any planned alterations before design or erection proceeds.
Confirm design status: either a recognised standard configuration whose assumptions are valid for the site, or a project-specific design and independent check by a competent person.

Obtain maximum leg reactions (including concentrated loads) and assess the supporting ground or structure. Treat basements, drains, manholes, voids, soft patches or recently backfilled ground as requiring specific assessment rather than assuming surface adequacy.
Verify that the tie strategy matches the actual façade, including openings, curtain walling, weak masonry or planned removals. Confirm anchor type, substrate suitability and any testing requirements.
Identify attachments (sheeting, netting, hoists, loading bays, fans, temporary roofs) as design inputs so that their effect on reactions, wind loading and restraint is allowed for before erection.

Establish change control so that any alteration to geometry, loading, restraint, exposure, foundations or supporting structure is referred to the Temporary Works Coordinator and re-checked where necessary before it is adopted.
Where the scaffold interfaces with public highways, excavations, deliveries or other temporary works, confirm licences, clearances and sequencing are compatible with the checked arrangement.

At permit-to-load or equivalent, confirm that the erected arrangement matches the design brief and checked design, including foundations, ties and attachments. Do not proceed until reviewed and accepted by the competent person under the project temporary works procedure.

body.p: Educational briefing only. Not for construction. Based on the Construction Magazine / London Construction Magazine article of 14 October 2026 and HSE scaffolding and temporary works guidance. It is not a design, a check or a statement that any particular scaffold arrangement is adequate or inadequate. No reactions, ground capacities or tie loads have been calculated here. Subject to project-specific verification and acceptance under the project temporary works procedure. AI-assisted drafting requires competent review before use on site.

posts.title: Late changes to erection sequences can leave beams vulnerable to lateral-torsional buckling
posts.excerpt: CROSS-UK Report 1479 (13 January 2026) describes a near-miss on a filler beam bridge deck. A late contractor change from lifting beams in connected pairs to lifting them individually introduced a critical temporary stability risk of lateral-torsional buckling under wet concrete. Utilisation exceeded 200% without bracing. The case underlines the need for early communication of temporary conditions, independent checking of sequence changes, and active Temporary Works Coordinator oversight so that temporary states are not assumed to be less critical than the permanent condition.
posts.linkedinReady:
Late changes to the intended construction sequence can introduce critical temporary stability risks that are not present in the final permanent condition.

CROSS-UK Report 1479 (published 13 January 2026) describes a near-miss on an approximately 20 m span filler beam bridge deck. Shortly before the Category II check was completed, the contractor altered the sequence from lifting steel beams in connected pairs (with precast concrete infill providing temporary stability) to lifting them individually. This created a significant risk of lateral-torsional buckling of the unbraced beams under the weight of wet concrete during construction. Assessment showed utilisation factors over 200% without rotational restraint at the flange ends or suitable bracing. Temporary LTB restraints were therefore necessary.

Even after the issue was identified, the contractor and temporary works designer later challenged the necessity of the bracing again, close to the concrete pour. By that stage reinforcement was largely fixed, restricting space for installation. The event was classified as a near-miss. It illustrates how late changes, unclear design responsibility for temporary conditions, and incomplete understanding of temporary stability modes can compress design and checking time and raise the risk of error.

HSE guidance on structural stability during alteration, demolition and dismantling is clear: temporary supports must be designed, installed and maintained to withstand foreseeable loads. Structures should never be overloaded. Temporary bracing or propping may be required where permanent elements that provide restraint are not yet in place or where the load path changes. Any temporary structure must be used only for the purposes for which it was designed. BS 5975-1:2024 provides the industry framework for managing temporary works, including the role of the Temporary Works Coordinator in ensuring clarity of responsibility and control of changes.

Provisional category only — to be confirmed by the TWC and the project temporary works procedure. Do not proceed until reviewed and accepted under the project temporary works procedure.

body.p: CROSS-UK Report 1479, published on 13 January 2026, concerns a filler beam bridge deck of approximately 20 m span. During the final stages of design and shortly before the Category II check was completed, the contractor changed the intended construction sequence. Instead of lifting steel beams in connected pairs (with the concrete infill precast to provide temporary stability for each pair), the beams were to be lifted individually. The change introduced a significant temporary stability concern: the risk of lateral-torsional buckling of the beams under the weight of the wet concrete applied during construction. The Category II checker identified that the main beams, if left unbraced and without rotational restraint at the ends of the flanges, could experience buckling under a utilisation factor of over 200%. Temporary LTB restraints were required. The designer confirmed this and notified the contractor. Later, approximately three months after the initial resolution and just two weeks before the deck concrete was scheduled to be cast, the contractor and their temporary works designer challenged the necessity of the temporary bracing again. Discussions involved commercial and programme considerations around design responsibility. Eventually the permanent works designer prepared a bracing scheme that tied the inner girders back to the precast edge beams, but by that stage most of the deck reinforcement had been fixed, restricting available space. The design and check programme was compressed. The reporter classified the event as a near-miss.

Temporary works provide an engineered solution to support or protect a structure during construction or to ensure stability while permanent elements are not yet providing their final restraint. CDM 2015 places duties on the principal contractor to plan, manage and monitor the construction phase, and on contractors to plan, manage and monitor their own work. HSE guidance on structural stability during alteration, demolition and dismantling states that temporary support must be designed, installed and maintained to withstand foreseeable loads and that structures should never be overloaded. Temporary bracing and propping may be required where the structure is subjected to changed load paths, where permanent bracing is not yet in place, or where the footprint or restraint changes during the work. HSE temporary works guidance further requires that any temporary structure is designed, installed and maintained to withstand any foreseeable loads and is only used for the purposes for which it was designed. BS 5975-1:2024 sets out management procedures for the control of temporary works as recognised industry good practice (it is not a statute). Late changes to erection or construction sequences can alter the temporary stability condition in ways that are not covered by the permanent works design assumptions. Independent checking and clear communication between permanent works designers, temporary works designers and the Temporary Works Coordinator are essential to identify such risks before they reach site. Provisional category only — to be confirmed by the TWC and the project temporary works procedure.

body.h: Practical TWC and TWS control points
ul: Ensure the design brief for temporary works explicitly addresses temporary stability at every stage of the construction sequence, including lifting, temporary placement, and before permanent restraint or bracing is effective.

Require that any proposed change to the construction sequence or method is referred to the Temporary Works Coordinator and the relevant designers before it is adopted. Changes that affect temporary stability must be subject to design and independent check.
Confirm that temporary bracing or restraint for lateral-torsional buckling (or other modes) has been designed for the actual temporary configuration, not assumed from the permanent condition.
Verify that responsibility for temporary condition design is clear between permanent works designer, temporary works designer and contractor, and that the TWC has oversight.
Where reinforcement or other permanent works have progressed, assess whether late introduction of bracing remains practical; if not, stop and review the sequence.
At permit-to-load or equivalent, confirm that installed temporary restraints match the checked design and that no unapproved changes have been made.
Treat late challenges to the necessity of temporary works as a trigger for formal review rather than informal agreement.
Do not proceed until the temporary stability arrangement, including any sequence changes, has been reviewed and accepted by the competent person under the project temporary works procedure.

body.p: Educational briefing only. Not for construction. Based on CROSS-UK Report 1479 and HSE guidance on temporary works and structural stability. It is not a design, a check or a statement that any particular temporary works arrangement is adequate or inadequate. No utilisation factors, bracing sizes or capacities have been calculated here. Subject to project-specific verification and acceptance under the project temporary works procedure. AI-assisted drafting requires competent review before use on site.

posts.title: Thermal spikes and soil desiccation can consume the capacity of temporary propping
posts.excerpt: Ground Engineering (9 October 2026) by Vicky Mastoridou CEng MICE of Groundforce Shorco examines how extreme heat and rapid wetting–drying cycles are challenging standard UK temporary works assumptions. In clay soils such as London Clay, prolonged desiccation followed by intense rainfall can produce rapid spikes in lateral earth pressure. Restrained steel props, sheet piles and bracing convert solar heating into additional compressive forces that consume the resistance reserves calculated under Eurocode 7. Design briefs, inspection regimes and monitoring need to recognise climate volatility rather than relying solely on historical averages.
posts.linkedinReady:
Thermal spikes and rapid soil moisture swings are no longer a distant climate footnote for temporary propping.

On 9 October 2026 Ground Engineering published an industry view by Vicky Mastoridou CEng MICE of Groundforce Shorco. It notes that record heatwaves and extreme wetting–drying cycles are forcing temporary works and shoring schemes to operate beyond the climatic envelopes assumed in design. In clay-rich ground such as London Clay, extended dry spells cause desiccation, cracking and temporary stiffening, followed by rapid water entry when rain returns. The result can be sudden increases in lateral earth pressure on retaining structures and their temporary supports.

Exposed steel props, sheet piles and bracing absorb solar radiation. Because they are restrained between walls, walers and slabs they cannot expand freely. The restraint converts into additional compressive axial force. A prop sized for earth pressures can therefore see a sharp load increase purely from thermal expansion, consuming part of the resistance reserve calculated under BS EN 1997 (Eurocode 7). Distinguishing genuine ground movement from a thermal spike requires careful interpretation of load-cell data.

HSE temporary works guidance requires any temporary structure to be designed, installed and maintained for foreseeable loads and used only for the purposes for which it was designed. BS 5975-1:2024 provides the management framework. When heat or rapid moisture change is foreseeable during the temporary state, it belongs in the design brief, the inspection and monitoring regime, and the triggers for review.

Provisional category only — to be confirmed by the TWC and the project temporary works procedure. Do not proceed until reviewed and accepted under the project temporary works procedure.

body.p: On 9 October 2026 Ground Engineering published an industry view by chartered civil engineer Vicky Mastoridou (CEng, MICE), development manager at Groundforce Shorco, titled “Redefining geotechnical limits: thermal loading and soil volatility in temporary works”. The article examines the geotechnical impact of extreme heat cycles on soil mechanics and the structural implications of thermal expansion in propping systems. It observes that with the summer of 2026 again surpassing previous temperature benchmarks, sustained thermal loads over 30 °C, widespread desiccation and shifting water tables can no longer be treated as short-term weather anomalies. Historical return periods based on past climate baselines cease to offer a reliable basis when extreme events recur. In clay-rich formations such as London Clay, extended dry spells cause the ground to shrink and crack, temporarily increasing stiffness while allowing movements that can affect foundations and excavations. When intense rainfall follows, water enters the cracks rapidly, producing localised softening, swelling and changes in pore-water conditions. Lateral earth pressures behind retaining structures can therefore spike more quickly than conventional design models anticipate. For temporary works this means ground parameters assumed at design stage may not remain valid during construction. Separately, exposed structural steelwork (heavy-duty hydraulic props, sheet piling and bracing frames) absorbs solar radiation, driving surface temperatures above ambient. Because these elements are restrained between retaining walls, walers and concrete slabs they cannot expand freely. The restraint converts thermal energy into compressive axial forces. A hydraulic prop operating under static earth pressures can experience a sharp load spike purely due to thermal expansion, transferring additional loading into the retaining structure and consuming part of the resistance reserve calculated under BS EN 1997 (Eurocode 7) partial factors. To accommodate the thermal component without exceeding design resistance, stronger, larger or denser propping layouts may be required, reducing working clearance. Distinguishing actual ground movement from thermal load spikes requires careful interpretation of telemetry from load cells.

Temporary works are an engineered solution used to support or protect a structure during construction, retain the sides of an excavation, or provide access. CDM 2015 requires the principal contractor to plan, manage and monitor the construction phase and requires contractors to plan, manage and monitor their own work. HSE temporary works guidance states that the law requires any temporary structure to be designed, installed and maintained to withstand any foreseeable loads which may be imposed on it and that it be only used for the purposes for which it was designed, installed and maintained. BS 5975-1:2024 sets out management procedures for the control of temporary works as industry good practice; it is not a statute. Exact clause references should be confirmed against the project’s licensed copy. Eurocode 7 (BS EN 1997) is the basis for geotechnical design of retaining structures and their temporary support, including consideration of actions arising from temperature changes in struts or props. When extreme heat or rapid wetting–drying cycles are foreseeable during the period of use, they are not external to the temporary works design. They can alter both the geotechnical loading (earth pressures, soil strength and stiffness) and the structural demand on restrained steelwork. Standard does not automatically mean low risk when the temporary state meets conditions outside the climatic envelope assumed in the original brief. Provisional category only — to be confirmed by the TWC and the project temporary works procedure.

body.h: Practical TWC and TWS control points
ul: State in the design brief the expected period of use, the range of ambient and surface temperatures that may be encountered, the ground conditions (including susceptibility to desiccation or rapid wetting), and whether thermal expansion of restrained props or frames has been considered.

Where clay soils or significant seasonal moisture change are present, treat ground parameters derived from site investigation as potentially time-dependent. Flag the need for observational monitoring or review if prolonged dry spells or intense rainfall occur during the temporary state.

Require the temporary works designer to identify whether thermal actions on props, walers or bracing are significant and how they have been allowed for in capacity checks (including any reduction in available geotechnical resistance).

Where load cells or other instrumentation are installed, establish clear thresholds and a protocol for distinguishing thermal spikes from genuine ground movement before operational interventions are made.

Include heat, desiccation or rapid wetting as review triggers under the project temporary works procedure. After a period of elevated temperature or intense rainfall, inspect and, where necessary, stop and review before continued reliance on the support system.

Confirm that any denser or stronger propping required to accommodate thermal effects still provides the required working space, access and plant logistics, or that the method has been adjusted accordingly.

At permit-to-load and during routine inspection, verify that the installed arrangement matches the design assumptions, including any measures (coating, shading, hydraulic compensation or monitoring) specified to manage thermal effects.
Do not proceed until the arrangement, including thermal and moisture assumptions, has been reviewed and accepted by the competent person under the project temporary works procedure.

body.p: Educational briefing only. Not for construction. Based on the Ground Engineering industry view of 9 October 2026 and HSE temporary works guidance. It is not a design, a check or a statement that any particular temporary works arrangement is adequate or inadequate. No loads, thermal increments, soil parameters or capacities have been calculated here. Subject to project-specific verification and acceptance under the project temporary works procedure. AI-assisted drafting requires competent review before use on site.
